ParallelVLM: Lossless Video-LLM Acceleration with Visual Alignment Aware Parallel Speculative Decoding

Quan Kong    Yuhao Shen    Yicheng Ji    Huan Li    Cong Wang Affiliation: Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China Affiliation: {qkv, riven, jiyicheng.cs, lihuan.cs, cwang85}@zju.edu.cn
Abstract

Although current Video-LLMs achieve impressive performance in video understanding tasks, their autoregressive decoding efficiency remains constrained by the massive number of video tokens. Visual token pruning can partially ease this bottleneck, yet existing approaches still suffer from information loss and yield only modest acceleration in decoding. In this paper, we propose ParallelVLM, a training-free draft-then-verify speculative decoding framework that overcomes both mutual waiting and limited speedup-ratio problems between draft and target models in long-video settings. ParallelVLM features two parallelized stages that maximize hardware utilization and incorporate an Unbiased Verifier-Guided Pruning strategy to better align the draft and target models by eliminating the positional bias in attention‑guided pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ParallelVLM effectively expands the draft window by 1.6∼1.8×1.6\sim 1.8\times with high accepted lengths, and accelerates various video understanding benchmarks by 3.36×\times on LLaVA-Onevision-72B and 2.42×\times on Qwen2.5-VL-32B compared with vanilla autoregressive decoding.

1 Introduction

The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) has ushered a new era in AI with foundational models like GPT-5, LLaMA, Qwen and Deepseek [1, 9, 40]. This success has quickly catalyzed multimodal research [28, 32, 22, 44], such as Video-LLMs [20, 26, 3], enabling a wide range of new applications like video understanding [12], content auditing [27], and autonomous driving [34].

Despite these advances, the practical deployement of Video‑LLMs is hampered by inference latency. State-of-the-art models like LLaVA-OneVision [20] typically encode videos into long sequences of visual tokens, which can easily scale from thousands to millions. Due to the quadratic computational cost of self-attention [41], such an explosion in token length creates a crippling performance bottleneck in both prefilling (KV cache computation) and decoding. To address this challenge, numerous efforts have been devoted to designing more effective visual token pruning methods [7, 50, 47, 39]. However, as shown in Fig. 1, since autoregressive access to the full model parameters is still required, they only offer limited acceleration. Even worse, pruning without validation induces inevitable distributional shifts that cause measurable performance degradation, particularly in fine-grained video understanding tasks.

To achieve lossless acceleration, Speculative Decoding (SD) offers a promising alternative [6, 19, 45] and SpecVLM has pioneered the application of SD to Video-LLMs [18]. As shown in Fig. 2 (a), SD replaces autoregressive decoding with a draft-then-verify paradigm, achieving a theoretical speedup proportional to the speed ratio of the draft/target model pairings. However, when applied to Video-LLMs, existing SD frameworks face two new challenges. (i) Sequential Execution: SD enforces strict sequential execution indicated by the idling gaps in Fig. 2 (a/b), which becomes costly with massive visual token prefixes in Video-LLMs. (ii) Entanglement between Speed Ratio and Model Alignment: visual tokens often contain substantial redundancy and the draft model can be pruned to improve the draft/target speed ratio. However, draft models with pruned visual tokens often struggle to retain both salient visual details and coherent textual grounding to align with the target model’s distribution. While SpecVLM attempts to guide the draft model pruning with the target’s attention scores [18], it suffers from the “positional bias” problem [11], which in turn hurts model alignment for videos rich in temporal and spatial semantic cues.

To address these challenges, we propose ParallelVLM, a co-design of parallel SD and draft video token pruning. Our framework combines prefilling/decoding parallelism and an Unbiased Verifier-Guided Pruning (UV-Prune) strategy to expand the draft window size without sacrificing alignment. As illustrated in Fig. 2 (c), ParallelVLM entails Parallel Prefilling (PP) and Parallel Decoding (PD) stages: 1) in PP, the draft model’s pruned prefilling executes concurrently with the target’s full prefilling, in which pruning decisions are guided by the vision-text variation signals from the target’s early-layer representations. This mitigates positional bias and hides the draft’s pruning/start‑up timing cost under the target’s latency. 2) In PD, draft token generation and target verification proceed in overlapping windows with an optimal window size determined by the enlarged draft/target speed ratio. The draft/target pairings also preserve a high accepted length with the alignment-aware design. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • ✧

    Systematic Analysis. We conduct a comprehensive analysis on SD efficiency for Video-LLMs, identifying the sequential execution bottleneck and the coupling relations between draft/target speed ratio and model alignment.

  • ✧

    Parallel Acceleration Framework. We propose ParallelVLM, a training-free and lossless architecture that leverages parallelism and unbiased pruning to expand the draft window while maintaining robust acceptance rates.

  • ✧

    Significant Speedups. Extensive experiments on five video understanding benchmarks show ParallelVLM achieves up to 3.36×\times and 2.42×\times speedups for the LLaVA-OneVision-72B and Qwen2.5-VL-32B respectively.

2 Preliminary

2.1 Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs)

A typical Video-LLM consists of: 1) a vision encoder EE that transforms input video frames into a sequence of feature vectors; 2) an adapter gθg_{\theta} that maps these visual features into the language model’s embedding space; and (3) a large language model that processes the combined multimodal input [20, 3]. Formally, a video input is processed into a sequence of visual tokens V1:m:=[V1,…,Vm]V_{1:m}:=[V_{1},...,V_{m}] and the text is tokenized into X1:n:=[X1,…,Xn]X_{1:n}:=[X_{1},...,X_{n}]. These sequences are concatenated to form a long, multimodal context prefix [V1:m,X1:n][V_{1:m},X_{1:n}], where mm could be much larger than nn for Video-LLM. Denote p⁡(⋅)p(\cdot) as the model distribution, then the subsequent text is generated autoregressively by conditioning on the text prefix of length k⁡(k≥n)k\ (k\geq n) :

Xk+1∼p(⋅|V1:m,X1:k).\displaystyle X_{k+1}\sim p(\ \cdot\ |V_{1:m},X_{1:k}). (1)

Current visual token pruning methods curtail the video tokens V1:mV_{1:m} before or inner LLM processing, changing the generated token distribution to Xk+1′∼p′(⋅|V1:m′,X1:k)X_{k+1}^{{}^{\prime}}\sim p^{{}^{\prime}}(\ \cdot\ |V_{1:m}^{{}^{\prime}},X_{1:k}), inevitably leading to performance degradation.

2.2 Speculative Decoding (SD)

SD accelerates autoregressive LLM inference without altering their output distribution [6, 19, 45]. The core of SD operates on a draft-then-verify principle: a lightweight draft model MqM_{q} generates γ\gamma candidate tokens. These tokens are then verified in a single, parallel forward pass by the more powerful target model MpM_{p}. Denote the single forward time of the draft and target model as TqT_{q} and TpT_{p}, respectively, then the speed ratio c=Tp/Tqc=T_{p}/T_{q} normally satisfies c≫1c\gg 1.

The lossless nature of SD is guaranteed by its verification mechanism. With accepted length kk, for each proposed token X^k+t\hat{X}_{k+t} in the draft sequence X^k+1:k+γ\hat{X}_{k+1:k+\gamma}, it is accepted with a probability determined by rejection sampling,

P(accept)=min{1,p(X^k+t|X1:k,X^k+1:k+t−1)q(X^k+t|X1:k,X^k+1:k+t−1)},\displaystyle P(\text{accept})=\mathrm{min}\left\{1,\frac{p(\hat{X}_{k+t}|X_{1:k},\hat{X}_{k+1:k+t-1})}{q(\hat{X}_{k+t}|X_{1:k},\hat{X}_{k+1:k+t-1})}\right\},

where p⁡(⋅)p(\cdot) and q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) are the probability distributions of the target and draft models. If X^k+t\hat{X}_{k+t} is rejected, then a new token is sampled from norm⁡(max⁡(0,p⁡(Xk+t)−q⁡(Xk+t)))\mathrm{norm}(\mathrm{max}(0,p(X_{k+t})-q(X_{k+t}))).

3 Why SD Falls Short for Video-LLMs?

Challenge 1: Sequential Execution Bottleneck. In vanilla SD, the draft and target models execute prefilling and decoding sequentially on the entire video token sequence. As shown in Fig. 3, the prefilling latency and decoding time become heavier with the increase of video tokens for both the draft and target models. For example, with 24​K24K video tokens, the target’s prefilling takes 44.2344.23 s, and the draft prefilling adds another 7.927.92 s. When it turns to decoding, the draft decoding time is Tq=78T_{q}=78 ms and the target decoding accounts for Tp=420T_{p}=420 ms. With a typical draft window size of γ=5\gamma=5 for the LLaVA-OV-7B/72B combination, the entire cycle takes γ⋅Tq+Tp≈2​Tp\gamma\cdot T_{q}+T_{p}\approx 2T_{p}. This means that the hardware remains idle for almost 20% of the span during prefilling and 50% during decoding due to sequential scheduling. As Video-LLMs require more powerful draft models to understand videos, the sequential waiting becomes even more expensive and persists as a fixed tax, whereas the vanilla SD provides no measure to “hide” this overhead.

Challenge 2: Entanglement between Speed Ratio cc and Model Alignment. The achievable acceleration in SD is governed by: (i) speedup ratio c=Tp/Tqc=T_{p}/T_{q}, which decides how many tokens can be speculated within the target’s verification time; (ii) model alignment between draft and target outputs, which controls the acceptance rates. Since video token sequences are known to have high redundancy [7, 4], TqT_{q} can be reduced by pruning the draft visual tokens to improve cc. However, a smaller draft model with pruned tokens often struggles to retain both salient visual details and coherent textual grounding to align with the target model’s full-context distribution. This consequently results in a sharp decrease of the acceptance rates.

To maintain alignment, effective signals from the target model should be utilized to guide the pruning process. SpecVLM [18] leverages attention scores as guidance [18]. Although seemingly intuitive, this approach is undermined by the positional bias phenomenon. As shown in Fig. 4, 21% of the attention-guided video tokens are chosen within only 4.0% position width (frames 1, 125-128) simply because they are “attention sinks” [46] or close to the text query [11], not because they are semantically important for visual reasoning and textual grounding. This is particularly problematic for video tasks where temporal coherence and mid-video content matter critically. In addition, attention-guided pruning is incompatible with FlashAttention [8] that adopts block-wise kernels without explicit computation of attention scores. This further prevents them from addressing the I/O bottleneck of Video-LLMs.

4 Design of ParallelVLM

4.1 UV-Prune: Unbiased Verifier-Guided Pruning

Instead of asking “which tokens does the model attend to”, we turn to answer “which tokens become increasingly aligned with the text query as information flows through the target model layers?” Tokens whose alignment with the textual query increases across layers are likely carrying task-essential semantics; conversely, tokens whose alignment stays flat or decreases are more likely redundant for the current query. This suggests a new pruning strategy that captures the semantics rather than raw attention scores. Hence, we utilize vision-text similarity variations of the token representations between the shallow layers as the criterion. Specifically, the vision-text similarity is defined as the cosine similarity between the prefilled video tokens ViV_{i} and text tokens XjX_{j} at the pre-defined early layer set l∈{1,…,L}l\in\{1,...,L\} from the target model:

𝒮i​j=Vi⋅Xj‖Vi‖​‖Xj‖,\small\mathcal{S}_{ij}=\frac{V_{i}\cdot X_{j}}{\|{V_{i}}\|\|{X_{j}}\|}, (2)

We then compute the similarity variation between consecutive layers and sum over all text tokens,

Δ​Si¯=∑j=1n∑l=1L(𝒮i​jl−𝒮i​jl−1).\small\overline{\Delta S_{i}}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{l=1}^{L}(\mathcal{S}_{ij}^{l}-\mathcal{S}_{ij}^{l-1}). (3)

A large positive Δ​Si¯\overline{\Delta S_{i}} indicates that video token ViV_{i} has gained cross-modal relevance through the network. Given a pruning ratio α⁡(0<α<1)\alpha\ (0<\alpha<1), we keep the Top-KK tokens,

V∗=𝐓𝐨𝐩𝐊⁡(Δ​S1¯,…,Δ​Sm¯).\small V^{*}=\mathbf{TopK}(\overline{\Delta S_{1}},...,\overline{\Delta S_{m}}). (4)

As shown in Fig. 5, the similarity variations are signals measured within the target model during its prefilling stage. Thus, pruning the draft model is directly guided by the target’s own semantics, which provides robust alignment and retains high acceptance rates. Unlike attention scores which bias toward early and query-adjacent tokens, our method reflects a knowledge transfer from the target to the draft model, without being constrained by absolute positions. This enables the natural retention of mid-video frames if there is relevance, preserving both spatial and temporal coherence.

4.2 ParallelVLM Pipeline

The ParallelVLM framework executes SD in two fully parallel stages with an overview shown in Fig. 5.

Stage I: Parallel Prefilling (PP)

➊ Execution Model. We launch two independent processes: 1) the target process prefills the full video token sequence V1:mV_{1:m} with the target model MpM_{p}; 2) the draft process only prefills the pruned video token sequence V∗V^{*} with the draft model MqM_{q}. Formally, we have:

Parallel{Draft: KVq←Mq(V∗,X1:n)Target: KVp←Mp(V1:m,X1:n),\small\text{Parallel}\begin{cases}\text{Draft: }\text{KV}_{q}\leftarrow M_{q}(V^{*},X_{1:n})\\ \text{Target: }\text{KV}_{p}\leftarrow M_{p}(V_{1:m},X_{1:n}),\end{cases}

in which X1:nX_{1:n} are the text tokens. Since the target prefilling latency is long, all draft-side operations including target-guided pruning, draft prefilling, startup token generation can be completed within this span. This completely hides the draft prefilling time and removes the sequential prefilling bottleneck in vanilla SD.

➋ Verifier-Guided Draft Model Pruning. Once the target process produce intermediate results of the pre-defined early layers, it broadcasts the target model’s layer-wise token representations to the draft process. The draft process then executes UV-Prune with pruning ratio α\alpha to select the top 1−α1-\alpha fraction of video tokens most relevant from the target’s perspective,

V∗=𝐔𝐕-𝐏𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐞(Mp(V1:m,X1:n),α).\small V^{*}=\mathbf{UV}\text{-}\mathbf{Prune}(M_{p}(V_{1:m},X_{1:n}),\alpha). (5)

➌ Startup Draft Tokens. The remaining idle time before target prefilling completes is used by the draft process to generate an initial speculative window of γ\gamma tokens. These startup tokens are immediately available for verification when Stage I ends, which guarantees that Stage II begins without a warm-up delay.

Results of Stage I: After parallel prefilling, (i) the draft model is ready to generate tokens rapidly using the pruned video context. (ii) the target model holds full-context KV caches for lossless verification. (iii) A startup window (e.g., γ\gamma tokens) is already queued for the first verification round.

Stage II: Parallel Decoding (PD)

➍ Execution Model. The draft and target models operate in a coordinated pipeline: in decoding round ii with accepted prefix of length kk, the draft model MqM_{q} generates a window of γ\gamma candidate tokens X^k+γ+1:k+2​γ\hat{X}_{k+\gamma+1:k+2\gamma} from the pruned context V∗V^{*}; simultaneously, the target model MpM_{p} verifies γ\gamma tokens drafted in round i−1i-1 using the full context V1:mV_{1:m},

Parallel{Drafti:Xk+γ+t∼q(⋅|V∗,X1:k+γ+t−1)Verifyi−1:Xk+1:k+γ∼p(⋅|V1:m,X1:k)\small\text{Parallel}\begin{cases}\text{Draft}_{i}:\hskip 9.24994ptX_{k+\gamma+t}\sim q(\cdot|V^{*},X_{1:k+\gamma+t-1})\\ \text{Verify}_{i-1}:X_{k+1:k+\gamma}\sim p(\cdot|V_{1:m},X_{1:k})\end{cases}

For t=1,…,γt=1,...,\gamma, each candidate token X^k+γ+t\hat{X}_{k+\gamma+t} is accepted with rejection sampling illustrated in Sec. 2.2. If a draft token fails verification, sampling resumes from the target distribution for that position. Then the pipeline performs pre-rollback and restart drafting [29].

➎ Window Size γ\gamma Selection. The optimal draft window size γ\gamma is determined by the pruned speed ratio c∗c^{*}:

γ=c∗=TpTq​(α).\small\gamma=c^{*}=\frac{T_{p}}{\ \ \ T_{q}(\alpha)}. (6)

Tq​(α)T_{q}(\alpha) is the draft decoding time at pruning ratio α\alpha and TpT_{p} is the target’s verification time with full contexts. As an example, without pruning: Tq=78T_{q}=78 ms, Tp=420T_{p}=420 ms, c=Tp/Tq≈5c=T_{p}/T_{q}\approx 5, so the optimal window size is γ=5\gamma=5; with pruning ratio α=0.9\alpha=0.9, Tq=47T_{q}=47 ms, Tp=420T_{p}=420 ms, c=Tp/Tq≈9c=T_{p}/T_{q}\approx 9, yielding γ=9\gamma=9, which is 1.8×1.8\times larger.

➏ Acceptance Rate τ\tau Dependency. The actual speedup depends on the pruning quality through acceptance rate τ\tau, τ=τ⁡(𝒫,α)\tau=\tau(\mathcal{P},\alpha). A well-algined pruning strategy 𝒫\mathcal{P} keeps τ\tau high even at aggressive pruning ratios (α=0.1\alpha=0.1).

4.3 Theoretical Speedup Analysis

ParallelVLM accelerates Video-LLMs by overlapping the draft and verification stages, and further addressing the visual redundancy of the draft model with the target’s alignment. If the original draft/target speed ratio is cc and the average acceptance rate is τ\tau, the theoretical speedup vs. autoregressive decoding is analyzed by the following theorem.

Theorem 1 (Speedup Ratio of ParallelVLM).

Denote the video token pruning method as 𝒫\mathcal{P} and the pruning ratio as α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1]. ParallelVLM overlaps the draft and verification stages, corresponding to an enlarged draft/target speed ratio c∗​(α)>cc^{*}(\alpha)>c, and a robust average acceptance rate τ^​(𝒫,α)\hat{\tau}(\mathcal{P},\alpha). For the draft window size of γ=c∗​(α)\gamma=c^{*}(\alpha), the speedup ratio of ParallelVLM is,

𝒱Vi​P​S​D=τ^​(𝒫,α)⋅γ⋅Tpγ⋅Tq​(α)=τ^​(𝒫,α)⋅c∗​(α).\displaystyle\small\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{Vi}PSD}=\frac{\hat{\tau}(\mathcal{P},\alpha)\cdot\gamma\cdot T_{p}}{\gamma\cdot T_{q}(\alpha)}=\hat{\tau}(\mathcal{P},\alpha)\cdot c^{*}(\alpha). (7)

With the optimal acceptance rate τ^​(𝒫,α)=1\hat{\tau}(\mathcal{P},\alpha)=1, 𝒱Vi​P​S​D=c∗​(α)\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{Vi}PSD}=c^{*}(\alpha) represents c∗​(α)c×\frac{c^{*}(\alpha)}{c}\times speedup than Parallel SD [29]. For example, the speedup is 1.8×1.8\times for LLaVA-OV-7B/72B and 1.6×1.6\times for Qwen2.5-VL-7B/32B. We refer to the Appendix for detailed proofs and a comprehensive comparison with vanilla SD.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setting

Baseline Methods. For Video-LLMs, autoregressive decoding (AR) is the default decoding setting (1.00×1.00\times baseline). We evaluate the proposed ParallelVLM against a series of lossless speculative decoding methods and lossy visual token pruning methods. For lossless speculative decoding, we include five methods, which are all plug-and-play with no need of model training.

  • ∙\bullet

    Vanilla SD [6]: Standard implementation where a draft model generates γ\gamma tokens for target verification.

  • ∙\bullet

    OnSD [15]: Light-weight text-only LLM as the draft model for VLM speculative decoding.

  • ∙\bullet

    SD-Tree [24]: Speculative decoding with a 5-layer draft tree structure for multi-branch candidate paths.

  • ∙\bullet

    SpecVLM [18]: Verifier’s attention-guided draft token pruning for improved Video-LLM speculative decoding.

  • ∙\bullet

    STD [49]: KV cache sparsification of the dense target as the draft model for Video-LLM speculative decoding.

For visual token pruning, we collect four dynamic methods that employ the intra-LLM information. We include one-stage importance ranking methods FastV [7], PDrop [47], and two-stage merge-then-sparsify methods SparseVLM [50], DyCoke [39]. Unlike lossless SD methods, pruning is directly performed on the target model.

Benchmarks and Metrics. Since ParallelVLM focuses on long‑paragraph decoding, we evaluate its performance in video captioning and video description tasks. The benchmarks we use include VideoDetailCaption [31], VideoMME [13], MVBench [21], MVLU [52] and LongVideoBench [43]. For metrics, we assess the acceleration effects with: (i) speedup ratio vs. the autoregressive baseline; (ii) the mean accepted length MM to reflect the speculation accuracy; (iii) token-wise acceptance ratio 𝒜\mathcal{A} to measure the distribution shifts of lossy visual pruning methods. Due to the lack of long, detailed ground truth description labels, we leverage the target model with full context for evaluation.

Implementation Details. Recall that the acceleration of SD mainly depends on the speedup ratio cc and alignment between the draft/target models. For comprehensive evaluation, we evaluate five draft/target pairings across LLaVA-OneVision [20] and Qwen2.5-VL [3], covering cc from 1−51-5 (rounded to nearest integer): (i) LLaVA-OV (0.50.5B & 77B, c=2c=2), (ii) LLaVA-OV (77B & 7272B, c=5c=5), (iii) Qwen2.5-VL (77B & 3232B: c=3c=3), (iv) LLaVA-OV (77B & 77B, c=1c=1), (v) Qwen2.5-VL (77B & 77B: c=1c=1). For LLaVA-OneVision, we sample 128128 frames for each video with a total of 196×128=25,088196\times 128=25,088 video tokens; for Qwen2.5-VL, we keep the same number of video tokens accordingly. The max output length is set to K=512K=512. All the experiments are conducted with 8×\times L40S GPUs.

5.2 Main Results

Comparison with Lossless SD Methods. While model combinations with different speed ratios cc greatly influence the overall acceleration, we observe three advantages of ParallelVLM over the baseline methods. (i) ParallelVLM achieves significantly better acceleration across the five combinations. As shown in Tab. 1, ParallelVLM achieves 2.11×\times, 3.36×\times and 2.42×\times acceleration on average for LLaVA-OV-0.50.5B/77B, LLaVA-OV-77B/7272B, Qwen2.5-VL-77B/3232B, respectively. Notably, ParallelVLM surpasses the existing SOTA SpecVLM [18] by 0.30∼0.64×0.30\sim 0.64\times, mainly attributed to the co-design of the parallel pipeline and UV-Pruning. (ii) ParallelVLM enables adaptive draft length MM with continuous draft stages. Unlike vanilla SD framework that requires sequential waiting for draft and verification, ParallelVLM facilitates continuous drafting and simultaneous verification with adaptive draft length [29]. As shown in Tab. 1, ParallelVLM maintains a considerable mean accepted length (MM) of 8.31,6.83,4.288.31,6.83,4.28 for the three combinations. The robust acceptance reduces unsuccessful speculation and rollbacks [37], ensuring the overall speedup performance. (iii) ParallelVLM makes Self-SD more effective in practice. Self-SD [49] is a special paradigm with perfect alignment traded by a smaller speed ratio cc. While vanilla SD methods wait for the draft model to finish, ParallelVLM verifies candidate tokens while drafting, greatly reducing unnecessary waiting time. As shown in the last two rows in Tab. 1, Self-SD achieves a mean accepted length of M>14M>14, with an acceleration of 1.51∼1.55×1.51\sim 1.55\times, which accounts for ∼0.30×\sim 0.30\times higher speedup than SpecVLM [18] and STD [49] methods.

Comparison with Lossy Visual Token Pruning Methods. Compared with vanilla visual token pruning methods [7, 50, 47, 39], ParallelVLM is favorable from the two following aspects. (i) ParallelVLM has a theoretically lossless guarantee. As shown in Tab. 2, although FastV [7], SparseVLM [50], P-Drop [47], DyCoke [39] can reduce video tokens without a draft-then-verify framework, they inevitably lead to performance degradation (−9.1%∼−17.7%-9.1\%\sim-17.7\%). Therefore, it is questionable for their practical applications, particularly in tasks demanding fine-grained details. In contrast, ParallelVLM presents little information loss with target model verification. (ii) ParallelVLM offers significantly higher speedup. While we also observe an alignment-speedup trade-off among visual token pruning methods in Tab. 2, they only provide 1.44∼1.64×1.44\sim 1.64\times decoding time acceleration. However, ParallelVLM delegates rapid proposals to the 7B draft model, delivering 3.36×3.36\times and 2.42×2.42\times decoding acceleration for 7272B and 3232B models, respectively.

5.3 Ablation Study

Effect of Pruning Ratio α\alpha. Tab. 3 and Fig.6 confirm that higher draft pruning ratios substantially increase the speed ratio in Eq. (6). As shown in Tab. 3, with the original speedup ratios of c={5,3}c=\left\{5,3\right\} for LLaVA-OV-7B/72B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B/32B, the speed ratio increases to c∗={7,4}c^{*}=\left\{7,4\right\} at α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and c∗={9,5}c^{*}=\left\{9,5\right\} at α=0.9\alpha=0.9, respectively. In ParallelVLM, a larger cc expands the optimal window size γ\gamma we can choose within a target model verification time. As shown in Fig. 6, the overall speedup performance increases from 2.94×2.94\times to 3.36×3.36\times for LLaVA-0V-7B/72B and from 2.08×2.08\times to 2.42×2.42\times when α\alpha increases from 0.00.0 to 0.90.9. The slight drop in MM at high α\alpha could be offset by the gains of larger γ\gamma. However, extreme pruning (α=1.0\alpha=1.0) breaks alignment and confirms the need for a balanced setting. We observe that α=0.9\alpha=0.9 strikes a reasonable balance between the expanded window size and model alignment.

Impact of Unbiased Verifier-Guided Pruning. As shown in Fig. 7 (a), UV-Prune effectively mitigates the positional bias of attention-guided pruning meanwhile selectively focusing on different visual cues across frames. In Fig. 7 (b), we further evaluate the alignment of different pruning methods and report the mean accepted length MM when α=0.9\alpha=0.9. For comparison, although SpecVLM [18] leverages the target model’s attention scores for guidance, it provides only partial accurate alignment due to positional bias and MM drops by 0.20.2. For other methods without verifier guidance, the accept length drops more sharply by 0.3∼0.50.3\sim 0.5. In contrast, UV-Prune consistently achieves a higher accepted length.

FlashAttention Compatibility. Because UV‑Prune does not rely on explicit attention‑score computation, it is fully compatible with FlashAttention [8]. Tab. 4 demonstrates increasing benefits with longer sequence lengths. At 2424K sequence length, FlashAttention adds 1.35×1.35\times extra speedup on top of ParallelVLM and at 3232K, the gain further reaches to 1.41×1.41\times. With an increasing demand for long video understanding tasks, the compatibility with efficient attention operators is increasingly important in the future.

6 Related Work

Visual Token Pruning for VLMs. A plethora of works have identified substantial redundancy in visual tokens and proposed pruning strategies to speed up VLMs. Existing approaches can generally be grouped into pre-LLM [48, 2, 33, 17, 36, 42, 30, 38] and intra-LLM pruning [7, 50, 47, 39]. The pre-LLM methods (e.g. PruMerge [33] and FastVID [36]) remove redundant tokens at the vision encoder stage before they are passed to the language model, leveraging fixed similarity or clustering criteria. Intra‑LLM methods (e.g. FastV [7], SparseVLM [50], PDrop [47], DyCoke [39]) dynamically prune or sparsify the KV cache during the LLM’s forward computation. Although visual token pruning methods reduce token load in long-video scenarios, they offer limited acceleration and cause inevitable distributional shifts that lead to performance degradation.

Speculative Decoding for LLMs and VLMs. SD utilizes a lightweight draft model to draft candidate tokens and verify them simultaneously [19, 45], thereby reducing the autoregressive latency of the target model. It can be categorized into draft model training-based [5, 10, 24, 23, 25] and training-free methods [14, 51, 6]. Subsequent works such as PEARL [29], SpecBranch [37] further explore parallel designs. When extended to VLMs, the draft model has been instantiated as a text-only model [15], a distilled model [16], or a lightweight “twig” model [35]. However, naive adaptations to VLM often overlook the fact that draft latency can grow significantly in long-context video understanding, where large amounts of visual tokens must be processed. As a result, current approaches are often ineffective [15] or inefficient [16, 35] for large-scale video inputs.

Speculative Decoding for Video-LLMs. The long-context video prefilling contradicts the principle of a lightweight draft model in speculative decoding. To address this challenge, Sparse-to-Dense (STD) [49] introduces a Self-SD framework and utilizes sparse KV cache selection of the dense target model to serve as the draft model. The closest work to ours is SpecVLM [18], which incorporates SD with attention-guided token pruning from the target model. In contrast to standard SD with sequential dependency, we enables complete parallelism while making video token pruning alignment-aware, unbiased and fully compatible with modern hardware optimizations like FlashAttention [8].

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose ParallelVLM to remove autoregressive decoding bottlenecks in Video-LLMs caused by massive video token inputs. It combines parallel prefilling and parallel decoding with UV-Prune, an attention-free, verifier-guided token reduction method using vision-text similarity variation. By co-designing with parallel SD, our framework improves the speedup ratio while preserving lossless generation, accelerating LLaVA-OV-72B and Qwen2.5-VL-32B by up to 3.36×3.36\times and 2.42×2.42\times, respectively.

Supplementary Material

For readers who are not familiar with speculative decoding and parallel decoding, we provide more detailed explanations in the appendix. The appendix is organized as follows: experimental details are presented in Sec. A, parallel decoding in Sec. B, and theoretical analysis of the proposed method in Sec. C. Additionally, we elaborate on the origin of the unbias nature of UV-Prune in Sec. D. Finally, we include several illustrative case studies in Sec. E.

A Experimental Details

Tasks and Metrics. Since speculative decoding [19, 45] focuses on accelerating long-paragraph decoding, we select five video understanding and description datasets VideoDetailCaption [31], VideoMME [13], MVBench [21], MVLU [52], LongVideoBench [43] with rich semantic information. We filter out videos shorter than one minute and randomly sample 50 samples from each dataset for evaluation. Unlike traditional Visual Question Answering (VQA) formats 11 1 Different from our finer-grained long-paragraph decoding setting, VQA evaluation suites like LMMs-Eval mainly focus on reality checking., we employ prompt engineering to generate finer-grained descriptions. For the lossy visual token pruning method, due to the lack of long, detailed ground truth description labels in the community, we save the autoregressive output texts after pruning and use the target model with full context to perform token-wise speculative sampling [19] to measure the acceptance rate 𝒜\mathcal{A}. This approach not only saves the cost of manual annotation, but also accurately reflects the distribution shifts of the pruned models.

Model Combinations. Regarding the model combinations, since ParallelVLM is a training-free method, aligning the draft model with the target model poses a challenge. We therefore select model combinations with different parameter sizes from the same series to ensure that the draft and target models have a basic alignment capability. In experiments we find that models from the LLaVA-OV [20] series exhibit a higher alignment (M=8.31M=8.31 for 0.5B/7B and M=6.83M=6.83 for 7B/72B), while Qwen2.5-VL [3] shows a relatively lower alignment (M=4.28M=4.28 for 7B/32B). Additionally, the 0.5B/7B combination within the LLaVA-OV series achieves better alignment than the 7B/72B combination, as the former has more similar model capacities and fine-tuning data scales. Although our approach is totally training-free, draft training-based methods [5, 24, 25] can be seamlessly integrated to achieve improved alignment and higher acceleration ratios in future work.

Window Size γ\gamma Selection. For simplicity of explanation in the main text, we directly rounded the speed ratio between the draft model and the target model c=Tp/Tqc=T_{p}/T_{q} to an integer value. In practice, their acceleration ratio is not strictly an integer. In Tab. 5, we present the exact acceleration ratios for all the five combinations. Rounding the window size up or down relative to the speed ratio cc are both reasonable options, the superiority between which depends on the relative magnitudes of the window size γ\gamma and the mean accepted length MM [29]. For combinations of LLaVA-OV-7B/72B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B/32B with aggressive window sizes and relatively conservative accepted lengths, rounding down to reduce mutual waiting is a wiser choice. For Self-SD with narrow window sizes and high accepted lengths, rounding up is a more sensible option.

Memory Consumption and Latency Breakdown. We report the peak memory usage and latency breakdown in Tab. 6. Although performing the draft/target forward functions simultaneously, ParallelVLM incurs no more memory footprint beyond vanilla SD with draft model pruning (+26+26 GB than autoregressive). Furthermore, ParallelVLM directly saves the draft model’s prefilling time with parallel prefilling (−7.92-7.92 s), and significantly accelerates the decoding speed through the visual alignment aware parallelism. Our approach achieves a notable 7.557.55 token/s throughput, which is 3.36×3.36\times faster than autoregressive decoding. While the throughput metric may vary on different devices, the speedup ratio will persist for methodological superiority.

Tree-Attention Integration. Applying a draft tree structure to speculative decoding can help improve the accepted length, but it is not feasible under a parallel architecture. The draft tree generates KV caches for multiple candidates, which constitutes a batch of additional overhead. This overhead grows exponentially with the depth hh of the tree during parallelization (even sparse trees [24] exhibit considerable growth). In vanilla speculative decoding, the depth of the draft tree is generally equal to the window size h=γh=\gamma. However, for parallel decoding, the depth of the draft tree depends on the adaptive draft length [29] and may increase hh by multiple times. To address the limitation of applying the tree structure to parallel decoding, SpecBranch [37] attempts to achieve a balance with a sparser “branch prediction” structure, which we anticipate will find broader applications in the future.

B Parallel Pipeline Details

For clarity, we collectively denote the prefix of visual-text tokens V1:m,X1:nV_{1:m},X_{1:n} as 𝐱\mathbf{x} here to describe the pipeline advancement and rollback mechanisms of parallel decoding.

As illustrated in Algorithm. 1, Parallel SD [29] sets two verification modes for the target model: (i) Pre-verify, which verifies the first draft token in advance, and (ii) Post-verify, which performs batch verification meanwhile generating new draft tokens. We elaborate on more details in the following with the illustrative example in Fig. 8 of decoding the sentence “The video uses ParallelVLM for speedup” with the window size γ=3\gamma=3.

At T=0T=0, both the draft model and the target model complete pre-filling, they output a bonus token and execute the initial Pre-verify. The Pre-verify verifies the first token “The” before the verification stage. Upon successful matching (accept “The”), the mode switches to Post-verify. From T=0∼3​tT=0\sim 3t, a window size of draft tokens “video uses Parallel” is waiting to be verified. The Post-verify checks them with batch parallelism, accepts them all, and maintains the Post-verify mode. From T=3​t∼6​tT=3t\sim 6t, another window size of draft tokens “VLM method with” is waiting to be verified. However, “method” is rejected by the target model, so a new token “for” is resampled from the target’s distribution. The KV cache of the draft model rollbacks to “VLM” and starts from “for” to draft new tokens, meanwhile the mode is reset back to Pre-verify. From T=6​t∼9​tT=6t\sim 9t, since there are no draft tokens left, the target model verifies the first draft token “a”. Unfortunately, the target model rejects it and thinks that the resampled “speedup” is a better choice. The KV cache of the draft model thus rollbacks to “for” and restarts from “speedup” to continue its drafting. The whole pipeline from T=0∼9​tT=0\sim 9t thus outputs “The video uses ParallelVLM for speedup” within only three target model verification times. The maximum adaptive draft length [29] here is 5, as “The video uses ParallelVLM” is continuous without interruption of the first two draft stages.

C Theoretical Analysis

Let Tq=tT_{q}=t be the single forward time of the draft model and Tp=c⋅tT_{p}=c\cdot t be the verification time of the target model. For a predefined hyperparameter γ\gamma to control window size, we derive the ideal and practical speedup ratio by calculating the per-token time, respectively.

Theorem 2 (Vanilla SD (Ideal)).

Under full acceptance of the γ\gamma draft tokens, the per-token time of vanilla SD is:

TS​D=γ⋅Tq+Tpγ+1=γ+cγ+1⋅t.\displaystyle\small T_{SD}=\frac{\gamma\cdot T_{q}+T_{p}}{\gamma+1}=\frac{\gamma+c}{\gamma+1}\cdot t. (8)

Thus, the ideal speedup ratio is 𝒱S​D=TpTS​D=c⋅γ+1γ+c\mathcal{V}_{SD}=\frac{T_{p}}{T_{SD}}=c\cdot\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma+c}.

Theorem 3 (Parallel SD (Ideal)).

Under full acceptance of the γ\gamma draft tokens, the per-token time of parallel SD is:

TP​S​D=max⁡(γ​t,ct)γ={t,γ≥ccγ​t,γ<c\displaystyle\small T_{PSD}=\frac{\rm{max}(\gamma t,ct)}{\gamma}=\begin{cases}t,\ \ \ \hskip 9.24994pt\gamma\geq c\\ \frac{c}{\gamma}t,\hskip 9.24994pt\gamma<c\end{cases} (9)

When γ=c\gamma=c, the ideal speedup ratio is 𝒱P​S​D=TpTP​S​D=c\mathcal{V}_{PSD}=\frac{T_{p}}{T_{PSD}}=c, representing c×c\times speedup versus autoregressive decoding and 𝒱P​S​D/𝒱S​D=γ+cγ+1=2​cc+1→2{\mathcal{V}_{PSD}}/{\mathcal{V}_{SD}}=\frac{\gamma+c}{\gamma+1}=\frac{2c}{c+1}\rightarrow 2×\times (c≫1)(c\gg 1) speedup compared to vanilla SD. Note that 𝒱P​S​D\mathcal{V}_{PSD} can enjoy a higher gain of c∗>cc^{*}>c with our draft model pruning setting.

Theorem 4 (Vanilla SD (Practical)).

Under partial acceptance rate τ⁡(0<τ<1)\tau\ (0<\tau<1) of γ\gamma draft tokens, the per-token time of vanilla SD is:

TS​D=γ⋅Tq+Tpτ⋅γ+1=γ+cτ⋅γ+1⋅t.\displaystyle\small T_{SD}=\frac{\gamma\cdot T_{q}+T_{p}}{\tau\cdot\gamma+1}=\frac{\gamma+c}{\tau\cdot\gamma+1}\cdot t. (10)

Thus, the ideal speedup ratio is 𝒱S​D=TpTS​D=c⋅τ⋅γ+1γ+c\mathcal{V}_{SD}=\frac{T_{p}}{T_{SD}}=c\cdot\frac{\tau\cdot\gamma+1}{\gamma+c}, which increases monotonically with the acceptance rate τ\tau.

Theorem 5 (Parallel SD (Practical)).

Under partial acceptance rate τ⁡(0<τ<1)\tau\ (0<\tau<1) of γ\gamma draft tokens, the per-token time of parallel SD is:

TP​S​D=max⁡(γ​t,c​t)τ⋅γ={1τ​t,γ≥ccτ⋅γ​t,γ<c\displaystyle\small T_{PSD}=\frac{\mathrm{max}(\gamma t,ct)}{\tau\cdot\gamma}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\tau}t,\hskip 9.24994pt\gamma\geq c\\ \frac{c}{\tau\cdot\gamma}t,\hskip 9.24994pt\gamma<c\end{cases} (11)

When γ=c\gamma=c, the practical speedup ratio is 𝒱P​S​D=TpTP​S​D=τ⋅c\mathcal{V}_{PSD}=\frac{T_{p}}{T_{PSD}}=\tau\cdot c, which also increases monotonically with the acceptance rate τ\tau. Recall that Theorem. 1 gives 𝒱Vi​P​S​D=τ^​(𝒫,α)⋅c∗​(α)\mathcal{V}_{\text{Vi}PSD}=\hat{\tau}(\mathcal{P},\alpha)\cdot c^{*}(\alpha). It represents an expanded speed ratio c∗​(α)>cc^{*}(\alpha)>c with a robust acceptance rate τ^​(𝒫,α)\hat{\tau}(\mathcal{P},\alpha), where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the visual alignment aware pruning and α\alpha is the pruning ratio. 𝒱Vi​P​S​D\mathcal{V}_{\text{Vi}PSD} strikes a balance between c∗​(α)c^{*}(\alpha) and τ^​(𝒫,α)\hat{\tau}(\mathcal{P},\alpha) that exceeds 𝒱P​S​D\mathcal{V}_{PSD} by up to 0.3∼0.4×0.3\sim 0.4\times (see Fig. 6 (a)).

Although Theorem. 2 - 5 provide general illustrations, the theoretical speedup ratio of parallel decoding is actually more complex in practice. As described in Sec. B, the above theory holds only in Post-verify mode; however, if pre-verify (resulting from rollbacks) is taken into account, analysis must be conducted based on the distribution of accepted lengths. D Why is UV-Prune Essential?

In recent years, numerous studies have focused on pruning VLMs [7, 47, 39, 50] to achieve inference acceleration at the cost of a certain degree of generation quality. In contrast, our work explores the transfer of video-based understanding from more powerful target models to draft models, making it orthogonal to prior research. We retain the full context of the target model to ensure theoretically lossless generation, and perform pruning on the draft model to align with the target model – marking the first application in parallel decoding framework to allow window size expansion.

Feather [11] has discussed the issue of positional bias in the image domain. They observe that the shallow layers of LLMs serve as “active” regions for visual token comprehension and attribute the attention bias at the vision-text boundaries to the more similar RoPE positional encodings. By computing attention scores without positional encodings as the criterion, they achieve better performance gains.

However, directly applying Feather’s method is no longer feasible for the target model to guide the draft model pruning. The target and draft models differ greatly in embedding dimensions and network depth, leading to architectural mismatch when performing intra-LLM pruning directly on the draft model. In addition, Feather [11] requires re-computation of the target model’s attention scores without RoPE, which is not only time-consuming but also conflicts with FlashAttention [8].

To avoid introducing additional computations and ensure compatibility with FlashAttention, we adopt token representations from the shallow layers of the target model as the pruning anchors. Since attention itself is a similarity weight, using cross-modal (vision-text) similarity is a well-motivated approach. To further eliminate the bias induced by positional encodings, we calculate the similarity variations of visual tokens at each position layer by layer to “offset” the interference of positional encodings. In this way, UV-Prune accurately identifies the few key video tokens prioritized by the target model among a large number of tokens, and effectively transfers this focus to the draft model, achieving salient yet robust image-text relevance.

As shown in Fig. 9, both variation and similarity enhance the effectiveness of video token selection. The variation mechanism of UV-Prune mitigates “positional bias”, leading to significant improvements for both attention and similarity criterion. We also observe that similarity-variation converges at L=20L=20 (and it generalizes well for different model combinations). Thus, we predefine L=20L=20 as the number of layers for the target model to guide the draft model’s pruning. The propagation of token representations in such shallow layers consumes negligible transmission time (∼0.01\sim 0.01 s) and ensures that the subsequent pre-filling of the draft model is fully hidden within the target model’s pre-filling span. Most importantly, our alignment-aware pruning method meets the requirement for robust acceptance rates specified in Theorem 6.

E Case Study

We present two generation paragraphs in Fig. 10 (LLaVA-7B/72B) and Fig. 11 (Qwen2.5-VL-7B/32B) to intuitively demonstrate the effects of unbiased pruning guided by the target model in long-sequence video tokens, as well as the lossless generation performance of ParallelVLM compared to lossy visual token pruning schemes. We observe that ParallelVLM maintains finer-grained details and accurately reflects the realities in the videos.
